newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan CPC confirms problem at Taoyuan oil port.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan CPC confirms problem at Taoyuan oil port.

text.p: Taiwan's state-owned Chinese Petroleum confirmed on Wednesday that a broken cable at its northern crude port had stalled offloading and that part of its adjacent Taoyuan refinery could not reopen as planned.
"A cable connecting the offloading unit and the oil tanker snapped on Wednesday," a Chinese Petroleum official said.

The break was yet another setback for the 300,000 tonne tanker Vanadis, which suffered an eight-day delay in offloading its cargo after unspecified pipeline problems shut down both of the port's offshore units on September 15.
One of two crude unloading units was fixed and reopended on Monday, enabling the Vanadis to pump 200,000 tonnes, but rough seas and poor weather forced it to stop later the same day.
Operators tried on Wednesday to unload the final 100,000 tonnes but the cable break halted the effort.
The shutdown had immediate ripple effects, forcing a delay in offloading of another 300,000-tonne tanker, Arcadian, which was anchored nearby.
Chinese Petroleum sources in Singapore said a third tanker also was waiting to offload at Taoyuan.
Concern over low crude supplies at the Taoyuan refinery forced Chinese Petroleum to shut one of its two distillation or topping units to slow production.
Refinery operators had planned to restart the stalled topping unit on Wednesday or Thursday, assuming the port could provide new supplies of crude.

The Chinese Petroleum official confirmed that the cable break would delay the reopening of the topping unit, but would not comment on a report from a company source in Singapore that the delay could be five days or more.
The company official said the Taoyuan refinery has more than 300,000 tonnes of high-sulfur crude and about 200,000 tonnes of low-sulfur crude on hand.
A Chinese Petroleum engineer reached by telephone at the Taoyuan refinery said only one of four pipelines that connect the two unloading units to shore had been repaired.
Even if operators managed to restart offloading, the pumping rate would be only half of normal, doubling the time needed to unload a cargo of crude, he said.
